August mental health reset, mental healt.body:
Feeling like summer has passed too quickly? Discover how an August mental health reset can help you manage anxiety, stress and overthinking and prepare for September with greater calm and confidence.

Where did the summer go?

August can be a strange month.

The days are still long, summer may still be in full swing, and there may be holidays, days out and opportunities to spend time outdoors.

But somewhere in the background, September is beginning to appear.

You might find yourself thinking:

“I haven't made the most of the summer.”

“Where has the year gone?”

“I need to get myself organised.”

“I should have achieved more by now.”

Or perhaps you're already thinking about everything September will bring — work, school, college, appointments, routines, responsibilities and everything else that may have been put on the back burner during the summer.

For some people, this can create a sense of pressure rather than excitement.

If you're feeling unsettled, overwhelmed or anxious as summer begins to wind down, you're certainly not alone.

Rather than seeing August as a month when you need to suddenly get your life together, perhaps you could use it as an opportunity for a gentle mental health reset.

You don't need to "fix" everything before September

One of the traps we can fall into is believing that we need to have everything figured out before a new month, season or chapter begins.

We may create a long list of things we need to change:

  • Get organised
  • Exercise more
  • Eat better
  • Get back into a routine
  • Stop procrastinating
  • Sort out our finances
  • Become more productive
  • Get on top of work
  • Spend more time with family
  • Make more plans
  • Worry less

The list can quickly become overwhelming.

And when we feel overwhelmed, we may actually find it harder to take action.

A CBT approach encourages us to look at the connection between our thoughts, feelings and behaviours.

For example:

Thought:
“I have so much to sort out before September.”

Feeling:
Anxious, overwhelmed or stressed.

Behaviour:
Avoiding things, procrastinating, scrolling on your phone or feeling unable to decide where to begin.

This can then reinforce the original thought:

“See? I can't even get organised.”

Instead, try reducing the size of the task.

Ask yourself:

“What is one small thing I can do today that would make tomorrow a little easier?”

You don't need to solve everything at once.

Your summer doesn't have to look like everyone else's

Social media can make comparison particularly difficult.

We may see holidays, family days out, weddings, concerts, meals, beautiful scenery and people appearing to have the perfect summer.

It can be easy to compare their highlights with our everyday reality.

You might think:

“Everyone else is having a better summer than me.”

“I'm not doing enough.”

“I should be happier.”

“I'm wasting the summer.”

But social media doesn't show the whole picture.

Someone else's holiday photographs don't tell you how they felt before or after the photograph was taken. They don't show their worries, difficult conversations, financial pressures, loneliness or uncertainty.

When you notice yourself comparing, try asking:

“What evidence do I have that I'm seeing the whole story?”

And perhaps more importantly:

“What would I choose to do with my time if I wasn't comparing my life to someone else's?”

That question can be surprisingly powerful.

Notice the "shoulds"

CBT can be particularly helpful for identifying unhelpful thinking patterns.

One that can become very noticeable during summer is “should” thinking.

You may notice thoughts such as:

  • “I should be enjoying myself.”
  • “I should have travelled more.”
  • “I should have achieved more.”
  • “I should be more relaxed.”
  • “I should be spending more time with people.”
  • “I shouldn't be feeling anxious.”
  • “I should be further ahead in my life.”

The problem with “should” is that it can turn a preference into a rule.

Instead of:

“I should be enjoying every minute of summer.”

Try:

“I'd like to enjoy my summer, but I won't enjoy every day — and that's okay.”

Instead of:

“I should have achieved more.”

Try:

“I can acknowledge what I've managed this year and decide what matters to me next.”

This isn't about replacing every negative thought with an unrealistically positive one.

It's about developing a more balanced and compassionate way of thinking.

Create a gentle routine rather than a strict one

Summer often means routines change.

You may stay up later, sleep differently, take holidays, have different working hours or simply have a more relaxed approach to your days.

There is nothing wrong with that.

However, if you notice yourself feeling unsettled, gradually bringing a little structure back into your day can help.

You don't need a rigid timetable.

Start with a few anchors.

For example:

Morning:
Get up around a similar time and avoid immediately reaching for your phone.

Daytime:
Include some movement, fresh air or time outside if possible.

Evening:
Create a wind-down routine that gives your mind an opportunity to slow down.

Sleep:
Try to keep your sleep and wake times reasonably consistent.

The HSE highlights the importance of healthy habits and routines as part of supporting mental wellbeing.

Think structure, not perfection.

If you have a day where everything goes out the window, you haven't failed.

You simply begin again the next day.

Don't turn your August reset into another source of stress

There is a danger that a blog about a “reset” can accidentally become another productivity checklist.

That's not what this is about.

A mental health reset isn't:

“How much can I achieve before September?”

It's more about asking:

“What do I need more of, and what do I need less of?”

Perhaps you need:

  • More rest
  • More time outdoors
  • More connection
  • More boundaries
  • More enjoyable activities
  • More compassion towards yourself

And perhaps you need less:

  • Comparing yourself to others
  • Overthinking
  • People-pleasing
  • Saying yes when you mean no
  • Doom-scrolling
  • Criticising yourself
  • Trying to control things you cannot control

Your answers don't have to be dramatic.

Small changes can make a meaningful difference.

Try an August mental health check-in

Take ten minutes this week and ask yourself these questions:

1. What has been taking up most of my mental energy?

Is there something you've been worrying about repeatedly?

2. What am I telling myself about where I "should" be in life?

Notice the expectations you're placing on yourself.

3. What am I doing that genuinely helps me feel better?

This might be walking, talking to someone, spending time in nature, exercising, reading, mindfulness or simply having quiet time.

4. What am I doing that leaves me feeling worse?

Perhaps you're spending too much time comparing yourself to others, avoiding something important or repeatedly checking your phone.

5. What is one thing I could let go of?

It doesn't have to be a huge thing.

Maybe it's an unrealistic expectation.

6. What is one small thing I would like to carry into September?

Choose something realistic.

Perhaps it's going for a walk three times a week, protecting your evenings, practising a CBT technique or making more time for yourself.

You don't have to wait until September to start feeling better

Sometimes we tell ourselves:

“I'll deal with that in September.”

But if something has been bothering you for months, you don't necessarily have to wait for a new season before doing something about it.

You can start with one conversation.

One small change.

One appointment.

One decision to stop ignoring what you're feeling.

If you're experiencing persistent anxiety, stress, low mood, overthinking or low confidence, talking to a professional can provide a safe space to understand what's happening and explore different ways of coping.

CBT can help you identify patterns of thinking and behaviour that may be keeping you stuck and develop more helpful ways of responding.

At Breda Morrissey CBT & Counselling, I offer online counselling and CBT for adults across Ireland and the UK. Sessions are tailored to you rather than following a one-size-fits-all approach.

Your August doesn't need to be perfect

Perhaps the biggest reminder is this:

You don't need to make the rest of the summer count.

You don't need to squeeze every possible experience into August.

You don't need to become a completely different person before September.

And you don't need to have everything figured out.

You can simply pause.

Notice how you're doing.

Decide what matters.

Take one small step.

Then another.

Sometimes looking after your mental health isn't about making huge changes.

Sometimes it's about giving yourself permission to slow down, challenge an unhelpful thought, reconnect with what matters and remember that you are allowed to begin again at any time of year.

If you would like support

If anxiety, overthinking, stress or low confidence are making everyday life feel difficult, you don't have to work through everything alone.

I offer online CBT, counselling and psychotherapy across Ireland and the UK, providing a confidential and supportive space to explore what's going on and work towards meaningful change.

If you feel ready, you can get in touch to arrange an initial appointment or simply ask any questions you may have.

You don't have to have everything figured out before reaching out. Sometimes starting the conversation is the first step.

Coping with Exam Stress & Supporting a L.desc: Online CBT and counselling for anxiety, stress, and overwhelm. Compassionate, practical therapy for adults across Ireland.
Coping with Exam Stress & Supporting a L.body:
Coping with Exam Stress & Supporting a Loved One Through Exams

Exam season can bring a lot of pressure—not only for the person sitting the exams but also for the people around them. Whether you’re a student feeling overwhelmed or a parent, friend, or partner wanting to help, it’s important to understand how to manage stress in a healthy way and offer meaningful support.

Understanding Exam Stress

Exams can trigger a variety of stress responses—racing thoughts, sleep disturbances, low mood, irritability, or even panic attacks. For some, it’s the fear of failure. For others, it’s the pressure to succeed, comparing themselves to peers, or simply the volume of study.

While some stress can be motivating, too much can lead to burnout and poor performance.

Tips to Manage Exam Stress

  1. Set Realistic Goals
    Break revision into manageable chunks. Set daily targets instead of cramming. Celebrate small wins.
  2. Create a Study Routine
    A consistent routine builds focus and reduces anxiety. Include breaks, meals, and time for rest.
  3. Practice Mindfulness and Relaxation
    Techniques like deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, or even short meditations can help calm the nervous system.
  4. Get Active
    Physical movement, even a short walk, helps relieve tension and boosts mood.
  5. Sleep and Nutrition Matter
    Avoid all-nighters. A rested brain is far more effective. Eat nourishing meals to keep your energy steady.
  6. Challenge Negative Thinking
    CBT techniques can help reframe unhelpful thoughts:
  • "I always fail at exams" → "This subject is hard, but I’m doing my best and improving."

How to Support Someone Doing Exams

Watching someone you care about struggle with stress can be hard. Here’s how you can help:

  • Be Available Without Pushing
    Offer your support, but don’t pressure them to talk. Let them know you’re there when they’re ready.
  • Create a Calm Environment
    Reduce noise and distractions at home. Encourage a healthy study space.
  • Help With Practical Tasks
    Cooking meals, doing chores, or running errands can give them more time and mental space to study.
  • Avoid Adding Pressure
    Even well-meaning comments like “You’ll do great!” can feel like pressure. Instead, say:
    “No matter what happens, I’m proud of the effort you’re putting in.”
  • Encourage Breaks and Self-Care
    Remind them it’s okay to rest. Suggest a walk, a funny film, or a shared meal as a breather.
  • Look Out for Signs of Burnout
    If you notice signs of ongoing anxiety, low mood, or withdrawal, they may benefit from professional support.

﻿

When to Seek Professional Help

If exam stress feels unmanageable, or if it’s affecting sleep, appetite, relationships, or overall wellbeing, it might be time to speak with a counsellor.

At Breda Morrissey CBT and Counselling, I work with students and families to develop tools to manage stress, build self-confidence, and navigate the emotional challenges of exams.

You’re not alone, and you don’t have to struggle in silence.

To book a session or learn more about how CBT can help during exam season, get in touch today.

Do you over think_.html.title: Do you over think?
Do you over think_.html.desc: Online CBT and counselling for anxiety, stress, and overwhelm. Compassionate, practical therapy for adults across Ireland.
Do you over think_.html.body:
What happens when we overthink

Find out below & learn some techniques

[[IMG:Blue-Orange-Illustrative-Mental-Health-Infographic-Instagram-Post-1920w.png]]

When we overthink, our minds become trapped in a loop of excessive analysis and worry. This can lead to several mental, emotional, and even physical consequences, including:

  1. Increased anxiety and stress – Constantly ruminating on "what ifs" and worst-case scenarios can make you feel overwhelmed and tense.
  2. Paralysis by analysis – You may struggle to make decisions or take action because you're too focused on weighing every possibility.
  3. Sleep disturbances – Overthinking often leads to racing thoughts, especially at night, making it harder to fall or stay asleep.
  4. Reduced productivity – Time and energy are drained by overanalysing rather than doing.
  5. Negative self-talk – Overthinking can amplify self-doubt, guilt, or regret, often creating a distorted perception of reality.
  6. Relationship strain – Constantly rehashing conversations or worrying about others' opinions can create distance or misunderstandings.

Essentially, overthinking traps you in your head and keeps you from being fully present or confident in your actions.

1. Name the Thought
Label it: “That’s a worry thought,” or “That’s my inner critic talking.” Naming gives you distance and awareness.

2. Set a Worry Timer
Give yourself 10–15 minutes to worry intentionally. When the timer ends, gently bring your focus back to the present.

3. Ground in the Present
Use your senses:
👣 Feel your feet on the floor
🖐️ Hold something cold
🌬️ Take 4 slow breaths

Small shifts. Real impact.
You don’t have to stay stuck in your head.

Finding Calm in the Christmas Season.htm.title: Finding Calm in the Christmas Season
Finding Calm in the Christmas Season.htm.desc: Online CBT and counselling for anxiety, stress, and overwhelm. Compassionate, practical therapy for adults across Ireland.
Finding Calm in the Christmas Season.htm.body:
As the Christmas lights start to twinkle across our homes and towns, many of us feel a familiar mix of excitement, nostalgia… and maybe just a sprinkle of stress. The holiday season has a way of stirring everything up at once—joy, connection, pressure, memories, and the occasional urge to hide in the biscuit cupboard until January.

At Breda Morrissey CBT & Counselling, this time of year brings a gentle reminder: it’s okay if Christmas doesn’t feel perfect, polished, or peaceful 100% of the time. You’re human, and this season can be a lot.

The Emotional Cocktail of Christmas

Christmas often comes with:

  • The pressure to be cheerful and sociable
  • Family dynamics that would test even the most patient elf
  • Shopping lists that magically grow longer every day
  • Memories—both comforting and challenging
  • And the expectation to “hold it all together”

If this resonates, you’re not alone. Many people find December emotionally intense, even while genuinely enjoying the season.

A Little CBT Wisdom for the Holidays

Cognitive Behavioural Therapy encourages us to gently notice the thoughts that shape our feelings. This month, you might try:

⭐ Challenging the “shoulds.”
“I should be doing more.”
“I should feel happier.”
“I should have everything sorted by now.”
These thoughts pile unnecessary pressure on an already full season.

⭐ Creating small, manageable moments of calm.
A quiet cup of tea.
A walk in the crisp air.
Five slow breaths before facing the next festive task.

⭐ Being kind to yourself.
Your worth is not measured by how many presents you buy, how glowing your tree is, or how perfectly your plans turn out.

Sometimes “good enough” is more than enough.

Connection Over Perfection

The heart of Christmas isn’t about flawless routines or magazine-worthy celebrations—it’s about connection. With others, yes, but also with yourself. Allow space for rest, humour, and small joys. Laugh at the burnt mince pies. Let the wrapping be crooked. Embrace whatever your version of the season looks like this year.

If You Need Support, You’re Welcome Here

Whether Christmas lifts your spirits or brings emotional challenges to the surface, support is always available. At Breda Morrissey CBT & Counselling, you’ll find a warm, understanding, and down-to-earth space to explore whatever you’re carrying—at Christmas and all year round.

Wishing you a season filled with comfort, kindness, and moments of genuine peace.

Warmest Christmas wishes,
Breda Morrissey CBT & Counselling

How to Stop Overthinking.html.title: How to Stop Overthinking
How to Stop Overthinking.html.desc: Online CBT and counselling for anxiety, stress, and overwhelm. Compassionate, practical therapy for adults across Ireland.
How to Stop Overthinking.html.h1: How to Stop Overthinking Everything (Even When Your Mind Won’t Switch Off)
How to Stop Overthinking.html.body:
Even when your mind won't switch off

[[IMG:pexels-photo-7005411-1920w.jpeg]]

How to Stop Overthinking Everything (Even When Your Mind Won’t Switch Off)

Do you ever feel like your mind just won’t stop?

You replay conversations, imagine worst-case scenarios, and analyse every little detail—long after it’s over. Overthinking can feel exhausting, and no matter how hard you try, it can seem impossible to switch it off.

If this sounds familiar, you’re not alone. Many people struggle with overthinking, especially when they are feeling anxious, overwhelmed, or have been through difficult life experiences.

Why Do We Overthink?

Overthinking isn’t a flaw—it’s actually your mind trying to protect you.

When something in life feels uncertain or stressful, your brain goes into “problem-solving mode.” It tries to predict outcomes, avoid mistakes, and keep you safe.

But instead of helping, it often leads to:

  • Increased anxiety
  • Self-doubt
  • Difficulty making decisions
  • Feeling stuck or overwhelmed

The Problem with Overthinking

The more you think, the more you feel like you should be able to “figure it out.”

But overthinking doesn’t lead to clarity—it leads to confusion.

You may notice:

  • You go in circles without reaching a decision
  • Small worries become much bigger in your mind
  • You feel mentally drained

5 Ways to Gently Reduce Overthinking

1. Notice the Thought (Without Fighting It)

Instead of trying to stop the thought, try saying:

“I’m noticing I’m overthinking right now.”

This creates a small bit of distance and reduces its intensity.

2. Ask: “Is This Helpful?”

Not all thoughts are useful.

Gently ask yourself:

“Is this helping me right now?”

If the answer is no, give yourself permission to step away from it.

3. Set a “Worry Time”

Choose a 15-minute window each day to let your mind think freely.

When thoughts come up outside of that time, say:

“I’ll come back to this later.”

Over time, this helps your brain feel less urgency.

4. Bring Yourself Back to the Present

Overthinking pulls you into the past or future.

Ground yourself by noticing:

  • What you can see
  • What you can hear
  • What you can feel

Even a few seconds can help calm your mind.

5. Take One Small Action

Overthinking often leads to feeling stuck.

Ask yourself:

“What is one small step I can take right now?”

Action helps break the cycle.

You Don’t Have to Do This Alone

If overthinking is affecting your daily life, it can really help to talk it through with someone.

I offer online counselling for anxiety and overthinking across Ireland and the UK, providing a calm, supportive space where you can begin to understand your thoughts and feel more in control again.

Final Thought

Your mind isn’t working against you—it’s trying to protect you.

With the right support, you can learn how to step out of overthinking and feel calmer, clearer, and more like yourself again.

Supporting Dementia Caregivers_ A Guide.title: Supporting Dementia Caregivers: A Guide to CBT and ACT Therapies
Supporting Dementia Caregivers_ A Guide.desc: Online CBT and counselling for anxiety, stress, and overwhelm. Compassionate, practical therapy for adults across Ireland.
Supporting Dementia Caregivers_ A Guide.body:
Caring for a loved one with dementia is one of the most profound acts of love and dedication a person can undertake. Yet, it is also a journey that demands an immense physical, emotional, and psychological toll. When you are entirely focused on managing someone else’s changing reality, memory loss, and daily safety, it is incredibly easy for your own well-being to slip into the background.

At Breda Morrissey CBT and Counselling, I frequently meet caregivers who are operating on absolute empty. If you are caring for a partner, parent, or relative with dementia, please know this: feeling overwhelmed, exhausted, or even guilty does not mean you are failing. It means you are human, and you deserve support too.

﻿

The Invisible Weight of Caregiving

Dementia doesn't just impact the person diagnosed; it fundamentally changes the lives of their family members. Caregivers often experience what is known as "anticipatory grief"—grieving the loss of the person as they once were, even while they are still here.

Over time, the chronic stress of caregiving can manifest as:

  • Persistent Anxiety and Overthinking: Constantly worrying about what might happen next or whether you are doing enough.
  • The "Guilt Trap": Feeling guilty for wanting a break, losing your patience, or feeling resentful about the situation.
  • Physical Exhaustion and Isolation: Withdrawing from friends, hobbies, and social networks due to a lack of time or emotional energy.

If left unaddressed, this level of sustained stress can lead to burnout. Fortunately, evidence-based psychological therapies like Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) and Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) offer powerful tools to help you navigate these complex emotions.

How Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) Can Help

CBT is a practical, goal-oriented approach that looks at the relationship between our thoughts, feelings, and behaviours. For a dementia caregiver, CBT can be transformative in breaking unhelpful thinking loops:

  • Challenging "All-or-Nothing" Thoughts: Caregivers often hold themselves to impossible standards (e.g., "If I ask for respite care, I’m abandoning them"). CBT helps you identify these harsh assumptions and replace them with more balanced, realistic perspectives ("Taking a break allows me to be a healthier, more patient caregiver").
  • Managing Behavioral Triggers: Dementia can sometimes cause behavioral changes or confusion. CBT helps you step back, process your automatic emotional reactions, and find calmer, more problem-focused ways to respond.

How Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) Can Help

While CBT helps you manage your thinking, ACT focuses on changing your relationship with difficult emotions and situations. It is particularly effective for dementia care because it acknowledges a difficult truth: you cannot change the diagnosis, but you can change how you live alongside it.

  • Practicing Radical Acceptance: Acceptance doesn’t mean giving up. In ACT, it means stopping the exhausting internal battle against reality. Accepting that a situation is incredibly difficult—and that it’s okay to feel sad or angry about it—actually frees up emotional energy.
  • Reconnecting with Your Values: Caregiving can completely consume your identity. ACT helps you reconnect with what matters to you as an individual (e.g., connection, creativity, or self-care) and helps you find small, manageable ways to weave those values back into your week.
  • Mindfulness in the Present: ACT teaches you to drop an anchor in the present moment when the future feels too overwhelming to contemplate.

You Cannot Pour From an Empty Cup

Seeking therapy as a caregiver isn’t a sign that you can’t handle things; it is a vital strategy to ensure you can survive the journey intact. You deserve a dedicated, non-judgmental space to vent, process your grief, and learn how to hold boundaries for your own mental health.

If you are a caregiver navigating the ups and downs of a loved one's dementia journey, you don't have to carry the weight alone. Reach out today to explore how online sessions can provide the tools and support you need right from the comfort of home.

The Hidden Weight of Caring for Others.h.title: The Hidden Weight of Caring for Others
The Hidden Weight of Caring for Others.h.desc: Online CBT and counselling for anxiety, stress, and overwhelm. Compassionate, practical therapy for adults across Ireland.
The Hidden Weight of Caring for Others.h.body:
Caring for a loved one can be one of the most meaningful roles we take on in life. Whether you're supporting an ageing parent, a partner with a chronic illness, a child with additional needs, or someone going through cancer treatment, caregiving often comes from a place of love and commitment.

However, while caring for someone else, it's easy to lose sight of your own needs.

Many carers quietly carry an enormous emotional, physical, and mental burden. They may spend so much time focusing on another person's wellbeing that they neglect their own. Over time, this can have a significant impact on their health, relationships, and quality of life.

The Emotional Impact of Being a Carer

Being a carer can bring a wide range of emotions. Alongside love and compassion, many carers experience:

  • Stress and overwhelm
  • Anxiety about the future
  • Feelings of guilt when taking time for themselves
  • Frustration or resentment
  • Sadness, grief, and loss
  • Loneliness and isolation
  • Emotional exhaustion

Many carers feel they must remain strong at all times. They may worry that expressing their struggles means they are failing the person they care for. In reality, these feelings are a normal response to the demands of caregiving.

The Physical Toll

The impact of caregiving isn't only emotional. The ongoing demands can affect physical health too.

Many carers report:

  • Poor sleep
  • Fatigue and low energy
  • Increased stress levels
  • Changes in appetite
  • A weakened immune system
  • Headaches, muscle tension, and other stress-related symptoms

When someone is constantly focused on another person's needs, their own health appointments, exercise routines, hobbies, and social connections are often pushed aside.

When Your Identity Becomes "The Carer"

One of the less talked about challenges of caregiving is the loss of personal identity.

Over time, life can become centred around appointments, medications, responsibilities, and practical tasks. Many carers find themselves asking:

"Who am I outside of this role?"

The activities, friendships, and interests that once brought joy may gradually disappear, leaving carers feeling disconnected from themselves.

Signs You May Be Experiencing Carer Burnout

Carer burnout can develop slowly and may include:

  • Feeling constantly exhausted
  • Becoming irritable or emotionally reactive
  • Difficulty concentrating
  • Feeling detached or numb
  • Losing interest in activities you once enjoyed
  • Increased anxiety or low mood
  • Feeling hopeless or trapped

Recognising these signs early is important. Burnout is not a sign of weakness; it's often a sign that you've been carrying too much for too long without enough support.

Looking After Yourself While Caring for Others

Self-care is not selfish. It is essential.

Just as we are instructed to put on our own oxygen mask before helping others on an aeroplane, carers need to protect their own wellbeing in order to continue supporting those they love.

Here are some ways to begin:

Give Yourself Permission to Rest

Rest is not something that must be earned. Even short periods of downtime can help replenish emotional and physical energy.

Stay Connected

Isolation can intensify stress and emotional exhaustion. Try to maintain contact with supportive friends, family members, or support groups who understand what you're experiencing.

Accept Help

Many carers struggle to ask for help. If someone offers practical support, consider accepting it. Even small acts of assistance can make a meaningful difference.

Prioritise Small Moments of Self-Care

Self-care doesn't need to involve expensive retreats or hours of free time. A short walk, a cup of tea in peace, reading a few pages of a book, or practising mindfulness for ten minutes can help restore balance.

Acknowledge Your Feelings

It's okay to feel frustrated, tired, sad, or overwhelmed. Allowing yourself to recognise and process these emotions can reduce the burden of carrying them alone.

Consider Professional Support

Therapy can provide a safe, non-judgemental space to explore the challenges of caregiving. It offers an opportunity to process difficult emotions, manage stress, develop coping strategies, and reconnect with your own needs and identity.

Remember: You Matter Too

As a carer, you may spend much of your time ensuring that others are supported, comfortable, and cared for. But your wellbeing matters too.

Taking care of yourself is not a luxury or an act of selfishness. It is an essential part of maintaining your own health and resilience.

You deserve support, understanding, and compassion—not only from others, but from yourself.
